opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that the physical world itself is structured that way. If you think about what a robot actually has to do, there are decisions happening at very different speeds at the same time. At the lowest level you have motor control, which might be running at hundreds or even a thousand hertz: you're adjusting torques, reacting to contact, keeping balance. Then above that you have something like "I'm reaching for this cup," which unfolds over a second or two. And then above that you have the task-level plan, "I'm clearing the table" or "I'm making breakfast," which might span minutes or longer.

If you try to process all of that at a single resolution, you run into trouble either way. If you process everything at the finest time scale, the sequences get enormously long. A few minutes of high-frequency sensor data, video frames, proprioception, is a huge number of tokens, and with standard attention that cost grows quadratically. That's a big part of why I've been interested in efficient architectures: state space models, linear attention, hybrids. They let you handle much longer contexts cheaply. But even with efficient architectures, it's wasteful to treat every millisecond as equally important for high-level reasoning. You don't need to recall the exact joint angle from thirty seconds ago to decide what to do next; you need a compressed summary of what happened.

On the other hand, if you only process at a coarse resolution, you lose the fast reactive loop. You can't stop and think for half a second while a glass is slipping out of your gripper.

So the natural design is something hierarchical, and humans work roughly this way too. You have a fast, cheap, reactive system for low-level control, and a slower, more deliberate system that operates on compressed, abstracted representations for planning. The interesting research question is how you learn those abstractions end to end rather than hand-engineering them: how the model decides what to compress, what to keep at high resolution, and how information flows between the levels.

From the systems side, I think this is where hardware-aware design really matters. Robots have tight latency and power budgets; you often can't send everything to a giant model in the cloud. So getting architectures that are efficient at multiple time scales isn't just elegant, it's what makes these systems deployable at all.

r001.rationale: It says motor control runs at hundreds or even a thousand hertz and involves adjusting torques, clearly describing rapid action to control a robot’s joints.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the easiest way to see it is to look at how the physical world actually presents itself to a robot. You've got sensor streams coming in at very different rates. Joint encoders and IMUs might be giving you readings at hundreds or a thousand hertz. A camera is maybe thirty frames a second. And then there's the task-level stuff, like "pick up the cup and put it on the shelf," which plays out over seconds or tens of seconds. Those are just fundamentally different timescales, and if you force everything through one fixed resolution you're going to pay for it one way or another.

If you run everything at the fast rate, you're wasting an enormous amount of compute attending to high-level intent at a kilohertz when the intent isn't changing at a kilohertz. And if you run everything at the slow rate, you lose the fine-grained control you need for things like contact, where a few milliseconds actually matter. So you want some part of the system that's reacting very quickly to low-level signals, and some part that's reasoning over a much longer horizon about what the goal is and how the scene is evolving.

This actually connects a lot to what I care about on the sequence modeling side. One of the reasons I've been interested in state space models and recurrent-style architectures alongside attention is that they give you a natural way to compress the past into a state that persists across time steps. Attention is great when you need to go back and retrieve something specific, but it's expensive to do that at every step over a long history. A recurrent state is cheap to update and good at carrying forward a summary. So you can imagine a hierarchy where the fast loop is mostly state-based and reactive, and the slower loop occasionally does something more attention-like over a longer context. Mixing those is kind of the point.

There's also a language analogy I find useful. Language naturally has structure at the level of characters, words, sentences, documents. We've mostly ignored that and just tokenized into a flat sequence, and it's worked surprisingly well. But in robotics you don't get to do that as easily, because the different levels are genuinely tied to physical constraints. Your motor controller has to run at a certain frequency or the robot falls over. So the multi-resolution structure isn't a nice-to-have, it's imposed on you by the hardware and the physics.

And honestly, this is how biology does it too. You have reflexes that don't go through the brain at all, and then you have deliberate planning that's slow and expensive. Nobody thinks consciously about every muscle fiber when they reach for a glass. That separation is efficient, and I think the architectures that end up working for robots are going to reflect it, both in how they process inputs and in how they generate actions.

r001.rationale: The response says the motor controller must run at a certain frequency or the robot falls over, and describes a fast, reactive loop for low-level control.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s because different decisions require different amounts of detail and different reaction speeds. If a robot is about to collide with something, it needs to react very quickly. It shouldn’t have to finish reasoning about the entire task first. But if it’s planning how to move across a room or accomplish a sequence of steps, that requires a longer time horizon.

The same thing applies to spatial resolution. You might need a coarse view of the whole room to navigate, but a very detailed view of your hand and an object to grasp it. Processing everything at the highest resolution all the time would be expensive, and a lot of that computation wouldn’t help with the immediate decision.

So you want those levels to work together: a slower process that keeps track of the goal and the broader context, and faster processes that handle local feedback. The interesting challenge is how they communicate, so that a small, unexpected event can change the larger plan when it needs to.

r001.rationale: The response mentions rapid reactions and fast local feedback, but does not state that controlling a robot’s joints requires acting on a rapid time scale.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think robots have to deal with things that happen at very different speeds. If you’re trying to catch something or keep your balance, you need a very fast feedback loop. But if you’re planning how to move across a room or complete a task, that requires reasoning over a much longer time horizon.

And similarly, with resolution, you want a broad understanding of your surroundings, but when you’re manipulating an object, you might need very precise information about a small part of the scene. Processing everything at the highest resolution, at every time step, would be very expensive. So you want to maintain a coarse picture and selectively spend more computation where the details matter. The challenge is getting those different levels to communicate so that your longer-term plan can guide your actions, while fast feedback lets you adjust when something unexpected happens.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fast feedback for catching something or keeping balance, but it does not state that controlling a robot’s joints requires acting on a rapid time scale.
